newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright to discuss NATO expansion with Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Albright to discuss NATO expansion with Yeltsin.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright climaxes her first official talks with Russian leaders when she meets President Boris Yeltsin on Friday to put NATO's case for expansion and an unprecedented charter with Russia.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said initial talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Thursday were "very constructive and very detailed (and) both sides heard new things."

Neither he nor Albright gave details of the substance of the talks, which centred largely on European security issues and plans for next month's summit in Helsinki between Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Albright, who also met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, told reporters: "I think we had some good meetings. It was a matter of establishing a relationship and getting to know each other. Then we got down to work."
Albright, who is trying to assuage Russian concerns over NATO's plans to take in new members from central and eastern Europe, will be the first senior U.S. official to meet Yeltsin for seven months.

She is discussing a package of sweeteners intended to ease Russia's fears that its security could be threatened if the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation expands to include former members of the defunct Soviet-led Warsaw Pact.

The offers include a proposal for significant reductions in conventional arms in Europe and a charter defining NATO-Russia relations and creating a joint NATO-Russia brigade, mainly to be used in peacekeeping.
NATO allies presented proposals for major conventional arms cuts, amending a 1990 treaty, to a security summit in Vienna as part of the bid to appease Russia.
Some commentators had predicted that Albright, the first female U.S. secretary of state, would have a difficult time in Moscow because of her history.
She was born in Prague 59 years ago and fled with her family twice -- first for London to escape the Nazis and then to United States when Czechoslovakia fell to communism.

Before her visit, Moscow renewed its harsh rhetoric about Russia's implacable opposition to NATO expansion, the chief U.S. foreign policy goal this year. But U.S. officials indicated that her talks were held in a constructive atmosphere.
Burns said Primakov and Albright met privately for 90 minutes and later had a working dinner that was "very lighthearted and in which there were lots of jokes and toasts, lots of humour."
During her visit, Albright logged onto the Internet and a special State Department web site using a computer at Moscow's American Center Library.

Under a new feature on the site, called "travelling with the secretary of state," more than 3,000 schools in 48 countries can connect and "chat" with Albright about her travels. It is part of her campaign to stress the importance of diplomacy.
"I am halfway through my (nine-nation) trip. It is very hard work but also lots of fun," she told the students.
Questions flowed in from Germany, Finland, California and her alma mater, Kent Denver School in Englewood, Colorado, which asked what her dreams were as an immigrant schoolgirl.
"I never dreamed I could be secretary of state...My dream was to do well, speak English well, get good grades and start more international relations clubs as I did at Kent," she said.

Later, accompanied by a small crowd of reporters and photographers, she strolled the length of a nearly deserted moonlight-lit Red Square, freezing but still marvelling at the architecture of the Kremlin and St Basil's catherdral.
